problems.title: Pair Sum in a Sorted List
problems.statement:
You get a list of integers `nums` sorted from smallest to largest, and a number `target`.
Find the two different positions whose values add up to `target` and return them as `[i, j]` with `i < j`.

Exactly one such pair exists.
hints: Because the list is sorted, a sum that is too small can only grow by moving the left side right.
Start one pointer at each end.

approaches.name: Two Pointers
approaches.idea:
Put one pointer, L, on the smallest number and another, R, on the largest.

If their sum is too small, the only way to grow it is to move L to the right. If it is too big, move R to the left. Each step throws away one number that can never be part of the answer.

approaches.why: Each step moves one pointer inward, so we take at most n steps and only store two indexes.

problems.title: Palindrome After Cleanup
problems.statement:
A phrase counts as a palindrome if, after you ignore everything that is not a letter or a digit and treat
uppercase and lowercase as equal, it reads the same forwards and backwards.

Given a string `s`, return `true` if it is a palindrome under these rules.
hints: Compare characters from both ends.
Skip anything that is not a letter or digit before comparing.

approaches.name: Two Pointers
approaches.idea:
Put L at the start and R at the end. Skip over punctuation and spaces on either side.

When both point at letters or digits, compare them ignoring case. Any mismatch means it is not a palindrome. If the pointers meet, it is.

problems.title: Reverse Characters In Place
problems.statement:
You are given an array of characters `chars`. Reverse it **in place**: modify the array itself and use only
O(1) extra memory.
hints: Swap the first and last characters, then move inward.

approaches.name: Two Pointers
approaches.idea:
L starts at the front and R at the back. Swap the two characters, then step both pointers toward the middle.

When they meet, every character has been swapped into its mirrored position.

problems.title: Push Zeros to the End
problems.statement:
Rearrange the integer array `nums` **in place** so that every `0` ends up at the end, while all the
non-zero numbers keep their original relative order.
hints: Keep a write pointer for where the next non-zero number belongs.

approaches.name: Two Pointers (read & write)
approaches.idea:
Use a read pointer R that scans every number, and a write pointer W that marks where the next non-zero number should go.

Each time R finds a non-zero number, swap it into position W and move W forward. Zeros naturally drift to the end.

approaches.why: R passes over the array once; each swap is constant work.

problems.title: Remove Repeats From a Sorted List
problems.statement:
`nums` is sorted in non-decreasing order. Remove the repeated values **in place** so each distinct value appears
once, keeping the order. Return `k`, the number of distinct values; the first `k` slots of `nums` must hold them.

examples.why: k = 2 and the array starts with 1, 2.

hints: Duplicates are next to each other in a sorted array.
Write each new value at a write pointer.

approaches.name: Two Pointers (read & write)
approaches.idea:
The first value is always kept, so the write pointer W starts at 1. The read pointer R scans the rest.

Whenever R sees a value different from the last kept one, copy it to W and move W forward. At the end, W is the count of distinct values.

problems.title: Allow Each Value At Most Twice
problems.statement:
`nums` is sorted. Remove extra copies **in place** so every value appears at most twice, keeping the order.
Return `k`, the new length; the first `k` slots of `nums` must hold the result.
hints: Compare the new value with the one written two slots back.

approaches.name: Two Pointers (read & write)
approaches.idea:
Keep a write pointer W. A value may be written if fewer than two values are written so far, or if it differs from the value two slots behind W.

That single comparison guarantees no value appears three times in a row.

problems.title: Merge Two Sorted Lists Into the First
problems.statement:
`a` has length `m + n`: its first `m` values are sorted and the last `n` slots are zeros (free space).
`b` holds `n` sorted values. Merge `b` into `a` **in place** so that `a` becomes fully sorted.
hints: Filling from the front would overwrite values you still need.
Fill from the back with the larger of the two tails.

approaches.name: Two Pointers from the back
approaches.idea:
The free space is at the end of `a`, so fill the result from the back. I points at the last real value of `a`, J at the last value of `b`, and K at the slot to fill.

Put the larger of the two tails into slot K and move that pointer left. When `b` runs out, everything left in `a` is already in place.

problems.title: Squares in Sorted Order
problems.statement:
`nums` is sorted ascending and may contain negative numbers. Return a new array of the squares of each number,
also sorted ascending.
hints: The biggest square comes from one of the two ends.
Fill the answer from the back.

approaches.name: Two Pointers
approaches.idea:
The largest square is always at one of the two ends, because large negatives sit on the left and large positives on the right.

Compare the two ends, put the bigger square at the back of the result, and move that pointer inward. Repeat until the result is full.

problems.title: Biggest Water Tank
problems.statement:
`heights[i]` is the height of a vertical wall at position `i`. Choose two walls; together with the ground they
form a tank whose water level is limited by the shorter wall. Return the largest amount of water any pair can hold
(width × shorter height).
hints: Start with the widest tank.
Moving the taller wall can never help, so move the shorter one.

approaches.name: Two Pointers
approaches.idea:
Start with the widest tank: L at the first wall and R at the last. The water is limited by the shorter wall.

Moving the taller wall inward can only shrink the width without raising the limit, so always move the shorter wall. Track the best area as you go.

problems.title: Triples That Sum to Zero
problems.statement:
Return every distinct triple of values `[a, b, c]` from `nums` (using three different positions) with
`a + b + c = 0`. No triple may appear twice. Any order is accepted.
hints: Sort the numbers first.
Fix the first value, then solve a two-pointer pair sum on the rest.

approaches.name: Sort + Two Pointers
approaches.idea:
Sort the array. Fix the first number of the triple, then look for two numbers to its right that add up to minus that number, using L and R from both ends.

Skip values equal to the previous one so the same triple is never reported twice.

code.name: solution.py
Solution.java

approaches.why: Sorting is O(n log n); for each of the n fixed values the two-pointer scan is O(n).

problems.title: Triple Sum Closest to Target
problems.statement:
Pick three values at different positions of `nums` whose sum is as close as possible to `target`, and return
that sum. Exactly one closest sum exists.
hints: Same skeleton as the zero-sum triples.
Move L or R depending on whether the sum is below or above target.

approaches.name: Sort + Two Pointers
approaches.idea:
Sort, fix the first value, and use L and R on the remaining range. If the current sum is below the target, move L right to grow it; if above, move R left.

Remember whichever sum has been closest so far, and stop early on an exact hit.

problems.title: Sort Three Colors
problems.statement:
`nums` contains only `0`, `1` and `2` (three colors). Sort it **in place** in one pass so all 0s come first,
then the 1s, then the 2s, without using a library sort.
hints: Keep three regions: 0s on the left, 2s on the right, unknown in the middle.

approaches.name: Three Pointers
approaches.idea:
LO marks where the next 0 goes, HI where the next 2 goes, and MID scans the unknown middle.

A 0 is swapped down to LO, a 2 is swapped up to HI, and a 1 is simply skipped. Every element is placed in a single pass.

problems.title: Trapped Rainwater
problems.statement:
`height[i]` is the height of a bar of width 1. After rain, water collects between the bars. Return how many
units of water are trapped.
hints: Water above a bar = min(tallest on the left, tallest on the right) − its height.
The lower side decides, so process the side with the lower wall.

approaches.name: Two Pointers
approaches.idea:
Water above a bar depends on the shorter of the tallest bar to its left and the tallest to its right.

Keep L and R at the ends with the best height seen on each side. Whichever side is lower is the bottleneck, so its water is known right now: add it and move that pointer inward.

problems.title: Hidden Inside Another String
problems.statement:
Return `true` if you can obtain `s` from `t` by deleting some (or no) characters of `t` without reordering
the rest — in other words, if `s` is a subsequence of `t`.
hints: Walk through t once, matching characters of s in order.

approaches.name: Two Pointers
approaches.idea:
Pointer I tracks the next character of `s` we still need; pointer J scans `t`.

Whenever `t[j]` equals the needed character, I moves forward. If I reaches the end of `s`, every character was found in order.

problems.title: Rotate an Array to the Right
problems.statement:
Rotate `nums` to the right by `k` steps **in place**: each value moves `k` positions right, wrapping around
to the front. Use O(1) extra memory.
hints: Rotating by k is the same as rotating by k mod n.
Three reversals do the trick.

approaches.name: Reverse Three Times
approaches.idea:
Reverse the whole array, then reverse the first k values, then reverse the rest. Each reversal is a classic two-pointer swap from both ends.

The first reversal moves the last k values to the front (backwards); the next two put each part back in the right order.

problems.title: Fewest Rescue Boats
problems.statement:
`people[i]` is the weight of person `i`. Each boat carries at most two people and at most `limit` total weight.
Return the minimum number of boats needed to carry everyone. Nobody is heavier than `limit`.
hints: The heaviest person must leave on some boat; who can share it?
Pair the heaviest with the lightest if possible.

approaches.name: Sort + Two Pointers
approaches.idea:
Sort the weights. The heaviest person, at R, always needs a boat. If the lightest person, at L, fits alongside, they ride together.

Either way the heaviest leaves, so each step uses one boat and moves R left (and L right when they share).

problems.title: Palindrome With One Deletion
problems.statement: Return `true` if the lowercase string `s` can become a palindrome after deleting **at most one** character.
hints: Compare from both ends until the first mismatch.
At a mismatch, try skipping the left or the right character.

approaches.name: Two Pointers
approaches.idea:
Walk inward from both ends while the characters match. At the first mismatch we must delete one of the two characters.

So check whether the rest is a palindrome after skipping the left one, or after skipping the right one.

Reverse the order of the vowels (`a, e, i, o, u` in either case) in the string `s`, leaving every other
character where it is.
hints: Move pointers from both ends until each one sits on a vowel, then swap.

approaches.name: Two Pointers
approaches.idea:
L walks right and R walks left, each skipping consonants. When both sit on vowels, swap them and continue.

Strings are immutable in Java and Python, so we work on a character array copy.

problems.title: Equal After Backspaces
problems.statement:
In strings `s` and `t`, the character `#` means "backspace": it deletes the character typed before it (if any).
Return `true` if both strings produce the same text once typed out.
hints: Read both strings from the end.
Count pending backspaces to know which characters survive.

approaches.name: Two Pointers from the end
approaches.idea:
Scanning backwards, a `#` tells us to skip the next real character. So walk I down `s` and J down `t`, each time jumping to the next character that survives.

Compare the two survivors; any difference, or one string running out first, means the texts differ.

problems.title: Next Bigger Arrangement
problems.statement:
Rearrange `nums` **in place** into the next arrangement that is larger in dictionary order (the next
permutation). If `nums` is already the largest arrangement, rearrange it into the smallest one (sorted ascending).
hints: Find the first position from the right that is smaller than its right neighbour.
Swap it with the next larger value to its right, then reverse the tail.

approaches.name: Scan + Two Pointers
approaches.idea:
From the right, find the first value that is smaller than the value after it; this is the digit we must bump up. Swap it with the smallest larger value on its right.

The part after it is still in descending order, so reverse it with two pointers to make it as small as possible.

problems.title: The One Repeated Number
problems.statement:
`nums` has `n + 1` integers, each between `1` and `n`, so at least one value repeats. Exactly one value is
repeated (possibly many times). Return it without modifying `nums` and using only O(1) extra memory.
hints: Treat each value as a pointer to an index: i → nums[i].
A repeated value means two arrows enter the same index — a cycle.

approaches.name: Fast & Slow Pointers
approaches.idea:
Treat each value as an arrow to an index. Because two positions hold the same value, two arrows point at the same index, which creates a cycle whose entrance is the duplicate.

Move a slow pointer one hop and a fast pointer two hops until they meet. Then restart slow from the beginning and move both one hop at a time: they meet exactly at the duplicate.

approaches.why: Floyd's cycle detection takes linear time and just two variables.

problems.title: Common Values of Two Sorted Lists
problems.statement:
`a` and `b` are sorted ascending. Return the values they have in common, in ascending order. If a value appears
several times in both lists, include it as many times as it appears in both.
hints: Advance the pointer that sits on the smaller value.

approaches.name: Two Pointers
approaches.idea:
Put I at the start of `a` and J at the start of `b`. If the values are equal, it is a common value: record it and move both.

Otherwise the smaller value can't appear in the other list any more, so move the pointer that sits on it.

problems.title: Longest Stretch Without Repeats
problems.statement: Given a string `s`, return the length of the longest contiguous piece of `s` in which no character appears twice.

examples.why: "abc" has no repeats and nothing longer works.

hints: Keep a window with no repeats.
When a repeat enters, jump the left edge past the previous copy.

approaches.name: Sliding Window
approaches.idea:
Keep a window from L to R that never contains a repeat, and remember the last index where each character was seen.

When the new character at R was already seen inside the window, jump L just past that earlier copy. The window is valid again, so we update the best length.

code.name: solution.py
Solution.java

approaches.why: R visits every character once and L only moves forward, so the work is linear. The map holds at most one entry per distinct character, k.

problems.title: Best Sum of k in a Row
problems.statement: Given an integer array `nums` and a window size `k`, return the largest sum of any `k` consecutive numbers.
hints: Don't re-add k numbers for every window.
Sliding by one adds one number and removes one.

approaches.name: Fixed Sliding Window
approaches.idea:
Add up the first k numbers. To slide the window one step right, add the number that enters and subtract the number that leaves.

Each new window sum takes constant work, so we can check every window in one pass.

code.name: solution.py
code.src:
def best_window_sum(nums, k):
    window = sum(nums[:k])
    best = window
    for r in range(k, len(nums)):
        window += nums[r] - nums[r - k]
        best = max(best, window)
    return best

code.name: Solution.java

problems.title: Shortest Run Reaching a Target
problems.statement:
Given positive integers `nums` and a positive `target`, return the length of the shortest contiguous run whose
sum is **at least** `target`, or `0` if no run reaches it.
hints: All numbers are positive, so growing the window always raises the sum.
Once the sum is big enough, shrink from the left as far as possible.

approaches.name: Variable Sliding Window
approaches.idea:
Grow the window by moving R and adding numbers. As soon as the sum reaches the target, record the length, then shrink from the left to look for something shorter.

Because every number is positive, shrinking only lowers the sum, so we stop shrinking as soon as it falls below the target.

problems.title: Longest Same-Letter Run With k Changes
problems.statement:
`s` contains uppercase letters. You may change at most `k` characters to any other uppercase letter.
Return the length of the longest run of identical letters you can create.
hints: A window is fine if (window length − count of its most common letter) ≤ k.

approaches.name: Sliding Window
approaches.idea:
In a window, the letters we must change are all except the most common one. So a window is valid while its length minus the top count is at most k.

Grow the window with R. If it becomes invalid, slide L forward by one. The window never needs to shrink further, because only a bigger top count could give a longer answer.

problems.title: Scrambled Copy Inside
problems.statement:
Given lowercase strings `p` and `s`, return `true` if some contiguous part of `s` is a rearrangement
(permutation) of `p`.
hints: A permutation has exactly the same letter counts.
Slide a window of length p.length over s.

approaches.name: Fixed Sliding Window
approaches.idea:
Count the letters of `p`. Then slide a window of the same length over `s`, keeping letter counts for the window: add the letter entering on the right and remove the one leaving on the left.

Whenever the two count tables match, the window is a permutation of `p`.

Given lowercase strings `s` and `p`, return all start indices (in increasing order) of substrings of `s` that
are anagrams of `p`.
hints: Same window as checking for one permutation, but keep going and collect every match.

approaches.name: Fixed Sliding Window
approaches.idea: Slide a window of length `len(p)` across `s` while maintaining letter counts. After each slide, if the window counts equal the counts of `p`, the window's start index is an answer.

problems.title: Smallest Window Covering All Letters
problems.statement:
Given strings `s` and `t`, return the shortest substring of `s` that contains every character of `t`
(counting duplicates). If none exists return `""`. The answer is unique when it exists.
hints: Track how many required characters are still missing.
When nothing is missing, shrink from the left while it stays covered.

approaches.name: Sliding Window
approaches.idea:
Keep a count of how many of each character we still need, and a single number `missing` for the total.

Move R to grow the window. When `missing` hits zero the window covers `t`: record it, then move L to shrink until a needed character drops out. Repeat until R reaches the end.

problems.title: Longest Ones With k Flips
problems.statement:
`nums` contains only 0s and 1s. You may flip at most `k` zeros into ones. Return the length of the longest
run of consecutive 1s you can get.
hints: Find the longest window containing at most k zeros.

approaches.name: Sliding Window
approaches.idea:
Rephrase: find the longest window that contains at most k zeros, because those zeros can all be flipped.

Grow with R and count zeros. Whenever there are more than k, move L right until a zero leaves the window.

problems.statement:
Trees stand in a row and `fruits[i]` is the kind of fruit on tree `i`. You have two baskets, each holding one
kind of fruit (any amount). Starting at any tree and moving right, you pick one fruit per tree and must stop
when a tree's fruit fits in neither basket. Return the most fruits you can pick.

examples.why: Pick from trees 1 to 3: kinds 1 and 2.

hints: This is the longest window with at most two distinct values.

approaches.name: Sliding Window
approaches.idea:
We want the longest window with at most two different kinds. Count kinds in the window with a map.

When a third kind appears, move L forward and decrease counts until one kind disappears completely.

problems.title: Count Runs With a Small Product
problems.statement:
Given positive integers `nums` and an integer `k`, return how many contiguous subarrays have a product
strictly less than `k`.
hints: If a window has a small product, so does every window ending at R inside it.
Each step adds r − l + 1 new subarrays.

approaches.name: Sliding Window
approaches.idea:
Keep the product of the window from L to R. When it reaches k, divide out numbers from the left until it is small again.

Then every subarray that ends at R and starts anywhere from L to R qualifies: that's r − l + 1 new ones.

problems.statement:
A window of size `k` slides over `nums` from left to right, one position at a time. Return the maximum value
inside the window at each position.
hints: A value smaller than a newer value can never be a window maximum again.
Keep indexes in a deque with decreasing values.

Keep a deque of indexes whose values are decreasing from front to back. The front is always the current window's maximum.

When a new value arrives, pop smaller values off the back: they can never win again. Pop the front if it slid out of the window.

`prices[i]` is a stock's price on day `i`. Choose one day to buy and a **later** day to sell to maximise profit.
Return the maximum profit, or `0` if no profitable trade exists.
hints: Track the cheapest buying day seen so far.

approaches.name: Two Pointers (buy & sell)
approaches.idea:
Keep a BUY pointer on the cheapest day so far and let SELL scan forward. Together they form a window from buy day to sell day.

If SELL finds a cheaper price, it becomes the new buy day. Otherwise check the profit of selling today.

Keep a set with the last k values. If the current value is already in the set, its twin is at most k positions back.

After adding the current value, remove the value that just fell out of the window.

problems.title: Best Contiguous Sum
problems.statement: Return the largest sum of any non-empty contiguous subarray of `nums`.
hints: A window whose sum turned negative only hurts what comes next.

approaches.name: Sliding Window (Kadane)
approaches.idea:
Grow a window to the right and keep its sum. If the sum before adding the next number is negative, that prefix only drags things down, so restart the window at the current number.

The best window sum seen at any point is the answer. This is Kadane's algorithm seen as a sliding window.

problems.title: Take Cards From Both Ends
problems.statement:
Cards lie in a row with point values `cards`. You must take exactly `k` cards, each time from the left end or the
right end. Return the maximum total points.
hints: The cards you take are some from the left plus the rest from the right.
Start with all k from the left, then trade one left card for one right card at a time.

approaches.name: Sliding Window over the ends
approaches.idea:
Start by taking all k cards from the left. Then, one at a time, give back the last left card and take one more from the right end.

That slides a window of taken cards around the ends of the row; the best total along the way is the answer.

code.name: solution.py
code.src:
def card_points(cards, k):
    total = sum(cards[:k])
    best = total
    for i in range(1, k + 1):
        total += cards[-i] - cards[k - i]
        best = max(best, total)
    return best

problems.title: Product of Everything Else
problems.statement:
Return an array `res` where `res[i]` is the product of every element of `nums` except `nums[i]`.

hints: res[i] = (product of everything left of i) × (product of everything right of i).

approaches.name: Left & Right Running Products
approaches.idea:
The answer at i is the product of everything to its left times everything to its right.

First sweep left to right, writing the running product of the left side into the result. Then sweep right to left with a second running product for the right side, multiplying it in.

code.name: solution.py
code.src:
def product_except_self(nums):
    n = len(nums)
    res = [1] * n
    left = 1
    for i in range(n):
        res[i] = left
        left *= nums[i]
    right = 1
    for i in range(n - 1, -1, -1):
        res[i] *= right
        right *= nums[i]
    return res

problems.title: Count Runs Summing to k
problems.statement: Return the number of contiguous subarrays of `nums` whose sum equals `k`. Values may be negative.
constraints: negative values allowed, so a sliding window does not work
hints: A run (i..j] sums to k exactly when prefix[j] − prefix[i] = k.
Count earlier prefixes equal to prefix − k.

approaches.name: Prefix Sum + Hash Map
approaches.idea:
Keep the running prefix sum. A run ending here sums to k exactly when some earlier prefix equals current − k.

So store how many times each prefix sum has occurred, and add the count of current − k at every step. Start with prefix 0 seen once (the empty prefix).

code.name: solution.py
code.src:
def count_sum_k(nums, k):
    seen, prefix, count = {0: 1}, 0, 0
    for i, x in enumerate(nums):
        prefix += x
        count += seen.get(prefix - k, 0)
        seen[prefix] = seen.get(prefix, 0) + 1
    return count

approaches.why: Negative numbers break the sliding window's assumption that growing the window raises the sum, which is why we need the prefix map.

problems.title: Runs With Sum Divisible by k
problems.statement: Return the number of non-empty contiguous subarrays of `nums` whose sum is divisible by `k`.
hints: Two prefixes with the same remainder mod k bracket a divisible run.

approaches.name: Prefix Remainders
approaches.idea:
A run's sum is divisible by k exactly when the prefix sums before and after it leave the same remainder mod k.

Count remainders as we go; each new prefix forms a valid run with every earlier prefix that had the same remainder.

code.name: solution.py
code.src:
def divisible_runs(nums, k):
    seen = [0] * k
    seen[0] = 1
    rem = count = 0
    for i, x in enumerate(nums):
        rem = (rem + x) % k
        count += seen[rem]
        seen[rem] += 1
    return count

approaches.idea:
Use two pointers: `prev` starts empty and `cur` starts at the head.

At each node, remember the next node, flip `cur.next` to point back at `prev`, then slide both pointers one step forward. When `cur` falls off the end, `prev` is the new head.

code.name: solution.py
code.src:
def reverse_list(head):
    prev, cur = None, head
    while cur:
        nxt = cur.next
        cur.next = prev
        prev, cur = cur, nxt
    return prev

problems.title: Add Two Numbers Stored as Chains
problems.statement:
Two non-negative numbers are stored as linked lists of digits in **reverse** order (the head is the ones digit).
Return their sum as a linked list in the same format.
constraints: no leading zeros except the number 0
hints: Add digit by digit like on paper, carrying the tens.

approaches.name: Digit-by-Digit with Carry
approaches.idea:
Walk both lists together, adding the two digits and the carry. Write the ones digit into a new node and carry the tens to the next step.

Keep going while either list has digits left or a carry remains.

code.name: solution.py
code.src:
def add_chains(a, b):
    dummy = tail = ListNode()
    carry = 0
    while a or b or carry:
        total = carry + (a.val if a else 0) + (b.val if b else 0)
        carry, digit = divmod(total, 10)
        tail.next = ListNode(digit)
        tail = tail.next
        a, b = a.next if a else None, b.next if b else None
    return dummy.next

code.name: Solution.java

problems.title: Odd Positions, Then Even Positions
problems.statement:
Regroup the list so all nodes at odd positions (1st, 3rd, …) come first, followed by the nodes at even positions,
keeping the relative order within each group. Use O(1) extra space and return the head.
hints: Grow an odd chain and an even chain side by side, then join them.

approaches.name: Two Pointers (odd & even chains)
approaches.idea:
Keep two chains: `odd` starts at the first node and `even` at the second. Repeatedly link each to the node after the other, which leapfrogs them forward.

Finally connect the end of the odd chain to the head of the even chain.

code.name: solution.py
code.src:
def odd_even(head):
    if not head:
        return head
    odd, even = head, head.next
    even_head = even
    while even and even.next:
        odd.next = even.next
        odd = odd.next
        even.next = odd.next
        even = even.next
    odd.next = even_head
    return head

code.name: Solution.java

problems.title: Rotate a Chain to the Right
problems.statement: Rotate the linked list to the right by `k` places: the last `k` nodes move to the front. Return the new head.
hints: Only k mod length matters.
Close the list into a ring, then cut it at the right place.

approaches.name: Ring and Cut
approaches.idea: Find the length and the tail. Reduce k modulo the length, link the tail back to the head to form a ring, then walk to the node that should become the new tail and cut the ring after it.

code.name: solution.py
code.src:
def rotate_chain(head, k):
    if not head:
        return head
    n, tail = 1, head
    while tail.next:
        tail, n = tail.next, n + 1
    k %= n
    tail.next = head
    new_tail = head
    for _ in range(n - k - 1):
        new_tail = new_tail.next
    new_head = new_tail.next
    new_tail.next = None
    return new_head

code.name: Solution.java

problems.title: Swap Every Two Nodes
problems.statement: Swap every two adjacent nodes of the list (by relinking nodes, not by changing values) and return the head.
hints: Use a dummy node and a pointer to the node before each pair.

approaches.name: Pointer Rewiring
approaches.idea: Keep `prev` just before the next pair `a, b`. Rewire `prev → b → a → (rest)`, then move `prev` to `a`, which is now the second node of the swapped pair.

code.name: solution.py
code.src:
def swap_pairs(head):
    dummy = ListNode(0, head)
    prev = dummy
    while prev.next and prev.next.next:
        a, b = prev.next, prev.next.next
        prev.next, a.next, b.next = b, b.next, a
        prev = a
    return dummy.next

code.name: Solution.java
